idiom_name: instance variables of the smallest owning object; locals for transient values; in Hotwire UIs a Stimulus controller's value attributes on the element it decorates
implementation_notes: Ruby expresses colocation with instance variables on the smallest object that uses the value - a component, controller or presenter object - and with plain locals for transient values, so the state's lifetime is the object's lifetime. The replacement for the classic structure is this per-object ownership: class variables, module-level state and globals are shared across the whole process (class variables also across the class hierarchy), which is the Ruby shape of an app-level store and is justified only for genuinely process-wide values. In Rails/Hotwire front ends the ecosystem's realization is Stimulus: the controller decorates one element and keeps its state as typed value attributes on that element (with change callbacks), so the state is colocated with the element that uses it instead of with the page.
pitfalls: Class variables (@@) and globals are process-wide (class variables also shared across the hierarchy), so per-screen state placed there leaks between requests in a server process.
An unset instance variable reads as nil instead of raising, so a typo in a colocated attribute silently produces nil state instead of an error.
Blocks and Procs close over self, so a registered callback keeps the owning object alive after the screen has been discarded; deregister or use a weak reference when the listener outlives the view.
